section_summary: This section contains U.S. State Department records from 1942 to 1944 relating to Formosa (Taiwan), covering its history, colonial administration, and wartime legal status. It features a detailed February 1942 study assessing Japanese rule and future U.S. strategic interests, a 33-page historical chronology prepared by George H. Kerr of the Military Intelligence Service, and diplomatic correspondence on preferred English nomenclature. Later memoranda from June 1944 address post-war planning dilemmas concerning U.S. military government authority versus the transfer of sovereignty from Japan to China.

subfiles.about: A two-part State Department memorandum examining Formosa's historical background, Japanese colonial administration, and strategic post-war disposition.
subfiles.from: E. A. Low, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: This two-part study surveys Formosa's history under Dutch, Ming loyalist, Qing, and Japanese governance, detailing nineteenth-century foreign expeditions and American commercial interest. It reviews Japanese administrative mechanisms, tight police control, economic mobilization, and assimilation policies directed against the Chinese majority and aborigines. The memorandum concludes that Formosan resistance will emerge only upon major Japanese military defeats and recommends considering Chinese sovereignty paired with U.S. air and naval base rights.
subfiles.title: Formosa (Historical Sketch and Japanese Administration)
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations

subfiles.about: A memorandum circulating a comprehensive chronological outline of Formosan history prepared by George H. Kerr of the Military Intelligence Service.
subfiles.from: Max W. Bishop, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Max W. Bishop transmits a detailed 33-page historical outline compiled by George H. Kerr of MIS tracing the history of Taiwan from 1430 to 1942. The chronology records Dutch settlement, Koxinga's regime, Qing administrative policies, Western trade, missionary activity, and nineteenth-century naval clashes. It further chronicles the 1895 Republic of Formosa, Japanese pacification, tribal uprisings, early twentieth-century political and labor movements, and wartime conditions through 1942.
subfiles.title: Chronological Outline in Regard to Formosa

subfiles.about: A telegraphic instruction requesting the American Embassy in Chungking to ascertain official Chinese preference regarding the English names Taiwan or Formosa.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull instructs the Embassy in Chungking to make informal inquiries with the Chinese Foreign Office. The goal is to determine whether current official Chinese circles prefer the English designation 'Taiwan' or 'Formosa'. This instruction was intended to harmonize American official usage.
subfiles.title: Telegram to Amembassy Chungking, No. 505

subfiles.about: An internal memorandum discussing whether the U.S. Navy should be advised to adopt Taiwan as the official name in place of Formosa.
subfiles.from: Abbot Low Moffat, Division of Southeast Asian Affairs
subfiles.summary: Abbot Low Moffat reports on discussions in the Inter-Divisional Committee concerning official nomenclature for Taiwan. He notes Joseph Ballantine's view that Taiwan is the proper name, though formal advice to the Navy might be unnecessary. Moffat proposes sending a cable to Chungking to clarify the Chinese Government's preferred English usage before settling American terminology.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Official American Name of Taiwan
subfiles.to: John Carter Vincent, Division of Chinese Affairs

subfiles.about: A draft cable instructing the U.S. Embassy in Chungking to query the Chinese Government on its preferred English name for Taiwan/Formosa.
subfiles.from: Division of Chinese Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: This proposed cable instructs the Embassy at Chungking to promptly inquire whether the Chinese Government prefers 'Formosa' or 'Taiwan' as the official English version. It states that the United States will endeavor to secure uniform official use consistent with Chinese preference during the post-liberation period.
subfiles.title: Proposed Draft Cable to Chungking

subfiles.about: A telegram reporting the Chinese Political Vice Foreign Minister's opinion that Formosa is the preferred English designation.
subfiles.from: Clarence E. Gauss, American Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Clarence E. Gauss transmits the Chinese response to the State Department's inquiry regarding geographical nomenclature. He reports that the Political Vice Foreign Minister believes 'Formosa' is the English name generally preferred by the Chinese Government. The Vice Foreign Minister specifically cited the Cairo Declaration as authoritative support for this preference.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Chungking, No. 688

subfiles.about: A legal memorandum agreeing to adjust policy statements to avoid declaring that sovereignty over Formosa remains with Japan pending transfer.
subfiles.summary: Legal Adviser Green H. Hackworth accepts the formula proposed by Blakeslee and Ballantine regarding Formosan sovereignty. He notes that the principal concern was to avoid explicitly stating that sovereignty remains in Japan until formally transferred to China. Hackworth concludes that interim military administration will suffice for practical purposes without needing to resolve the abstract status of sovereignty.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Legal Sovereignty of Formosa
subfiles.to: George H. Blakeslee and Joseph W. Ballantine

subfiles.about: A memorandum recommending that U.S. military administration continue until Chinese sovereignty is restored, avoiding premature transfer of sovereignty.
subfiles.from: George H. Blakeslee (TS) and Joseph W. Ballantine (FE)
subfiles.summary: Blakeslee and Ballantine examine Assistant Secretary Breckinridge Long's objection to statements that Japanese sovereignty continues until formal legal transfer. They point out that an immediate transfer of sovereignty to the United Nations or China would undermine the U.S. Navy's supreme authority as military occupant under the Hague Convention. They recommend adopting policy language providing that American military administration of civil affairs will continue until Chinese sovereignty is restored.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Post-war Status and Military Government of Formosa
